results.result: A doctoral-level internship program (ImPACT) was developed at UNC Chapel Hill to provide customizable experiential learning opportunities for biomedical trainees. Over a 5-year period, 123 internships took place at over 70 partner sites representing at least 20 career paths. The program features 160-hour internships (full-time for 4 weeks or part-time over 2-3 months), requires written research advisor support and completion of qualifying exams, and typically occurs in the last 1-2 years before graduation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3 and C19-C24 provide consistent, detailed descriptions of the program's design, scope, and implementation. The data on program scale (123 internships, 70+ sites, 20+ career paths) is explicitly stated and internally consistent. The structural details (160 hours, timing, requirements) are clearly documented as program features.

results.result: Interns reported high satisfaction with the internship program, with 90% highly satisfied overall and 90% rating supervisor support as good or very good. Nearly all interns (95-97%) agreed the internship provided unique networking and professional development opportunities and increased their job market competitiveness. Pre-to-post surveys showed statistically significant increases (p<0.001) in understanding career benefits/challenges (48% to 97%) and awareness of career possibilities (59% to 97%). Notably, 42% reported improved research productivity and 33% reported improved research quality.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C38 present survey data with specific percentages and statistical tests. The pre-post comparisons include appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.001) and show large effect sizes. The data is internally consistent and supported by references to Figure 1. The response rates (61-73%) are adequate for the conclusions drawn.

results.result: Research advisors reported multiple benefits from the internship program. Nearly all (96%) indicated internships positively impacted interns' competitiveness for positions in the internship field, and 80% noted improved communication with their trainees. Focus group data from Years 1 and 5 revealed that internships helped trainees gain experience outside advisors' expertise, clarify career paths, and in some cases brought renewed enthusiasm and new techniques back to the lab. Benefits extended to lab culture, with internships demonstrating that trainees are valued and improving the research advisor's image.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C63 combine quantitative survey data (with specific percentages) and qualitative focus group findings. The mixed-methods approach strengthens the conclusions. The longitudinal focus group design (Year 1 and Year 5) with overlapping participants (5 of 7 original participants) provides valuable perspective on sustained impacts. The qualitative themes are supported by quotes in Figure 2.

results.result: Internship hosts were primarily motivated by mentoring fulfillment (89%) and attracting quality applicants (84%). Pre-to-post comparisons showed that hosting exceeded expectations in several areas: interacting with potential hires increased significantly (p<0.001), as did assistance with products (p<0.001) and gaining fresh ideas (p<0.05). Interestingly, mentoring fulfillment, while remaining high, showed a significant decrease from pre- to post-internship, suggesting hosting may have been less fulfilling than initially anticipated.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C72 present pre-post survey data from hosts with appropriate statistical testing. The finding that some benefits exceeded expectations while mentoring fulfillment decreased is nuanced and credible. The statistical significance levels are reported with p-values, and the interpretation acknowledges both positive and unexpected findings. Data is supported by Figures 1n-1u.

results.result: Logistic regression analysis demonstrated that internship participation significantly predicted career interest-job placement matches. Controlling for number of career interests and trainee type, interns were nearly three times more likely to match their career interests than non-interns (OR=2.99, p<0.001). The overall model was statistically significant (χ²=92.39, R²Nagelkerke=0.195, p<0.001). Descriptively, 39% of interns had exact matches versus 29% of non-interns. Post-hoc analyses including demographic variables showed female applicants were 1.5 times more likely to match career interests (OR=1.58, p=0.02), while race/ethnicity and citizenship did not impact the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C90 present a well-designed logistic regression analysis with appropriate controls and statistical reporting. The model includes relevant covariates (career interests, trainee type) and the effect size (OR=2.99) is substantial and statistically significant. The post-hoc demographic analyses appropriately test for equity concerns. The methods are clearly described in C74-C77, and the statistical results are properly reported with effect sizes, confidence intervals (Table 1), and p-values.

results.result: Graduate student interns showed substantially lower rates of postdoctoral training (36%) compared to non-interns (57%). Interns were more likely to enter for-profit sector positions (75% vs 42%) and less likely to enter academic positions (19% vs 46%). However, the authors acknowledge that interns are a self-selected population with career biases, being less likely to pursue academic tenure-track positions and more likely to have for-profit career aspirations.
results.evaluation: While claims C97-C106 present clear descriptive differences in career outcomes, the authors explicitly acknowledge self-selection bias (C99-C101), which is a critical limitation. The observed differences could be due to pre-existing career preferences rather than the internship effect. Without controlling for baseline career intentions or using propensity score matching, it's unclear whether the internship caused the lower postdoc rate or simply attracted trainees already planning non-academic careers. The descriptive data is accurate but causal interpretation is uncertain.

results.result: Analysis of trainee productivity showed no negative impact from internship participation. Interns (n=54) had slightly more first-author publications and slightly fewer total publications than controls (n=410), but neither difference was statistically significant (Table 6). Average time to degree was 67.1 months for interns versus 69.3 months for controls (p=0.09). These findings replicate previous work across 10 institutions showing no delay in graduate training or reduction in research productivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C111 present appropriate statistical comparisons (t-tests) with adequate sample sizes. The non-significant findings are properly interpreted as showing no evidence of harm rather than claiming equivalence. The replication of previous findings (C108, C111) strengthens confidence. The 2-year post-graduation requirement for inclusion ensures publications had time to appear. The statistical tests are appropriate for the data type.

results.result: Faculty attitudes toward internships improved significantly over 5 years. Independent samples t-tests showed significant increases in support for both 3-month internships (t(229)=2.54, p=0.01) and 1-month internships (t(212)=2.00, p<0.01). Support for 1-month internships reached 92% by Year 5. The proportion of faculty rating support as 'highly unlikely' or 'unlikely' decreased, while more moved from 'likely' to 'highly likely.'
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 present a clear pre-post comparison with appropriate statistical testing. The use of independent samples t-tests is appropriate given that individual faculty were not tracked. The effect is consistent across both internship durations and shows a clear positive trend. The data is supported by Figure 3. The 5-year timeframe allows for meaningful cultural change to occur.

results.result: Focus group methodology involved interviews with research advisors at two timepoints (Year 1 and Year 5). Seven faculty participated in Year 1, with five of the same seven participating in Year 5. The authors cite evidence that saturation can occur with as few as six interviews in homogeneous samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 describe the focus group methodology with appropriate detail. The sample size is justified by citation to Guest et al., 2006 regarding saturation in homogeneous samples. The longitudinal design with overlapping participants is a strength. However, the small sample size (n=5-7) limits generalizability, though this is appropriate for qualitative research focused on depth rather than breadth.

results.result: The study used a mixed-methods approach including surveys with closed- and open-ended responses and focus group interviews to assess benefits for interns, hosts, and research advisors. Survey response rates ranged from 61% for research advisors to 73% for hosts, with about 66% for interns.
results.evaluation: Claims C4 and C25 accurately describe the methodological approach and response rates. The response rates (61-73%) are adequate for survey research and comparable across stakeholder groups, reducing concerns about differential non-response bias. The mixed-methods design is appropriate for capturing both quantitative outcomes and qualitative experiences.

results.result: The ImPACT program has placed 175 interns with 80 partnering organizations since 2015 and is a major recruiting tool for UNC's life science PhD programs. The 1-month, full-time internship format is the preferred model of most research advisors, who noted it is simpler and least disruptive to lab progress. Survey data showed faculty support consistently dropped as proposed internship length increased from 1 to 3 months.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C130 combine program statistics with qualitative and quantitative data on stakeholder preferences. The preference for shorter internships is supported by both focus group data (C126-C128) and survey data showing declining support with increased duration (C129-C130, Figure 3). The consistency across data sources strengthens the conclusion about optimal internship structure.

results.result: Research advisors identified trainee characteristics and timing as important factors for internship success. They considered trainees' professionalism, time management, communication skills, and level of focus when determining internship appropriateness. Internships were seen as least disruptive when trainees were close to graduation and in the writing phase rather than actively conducting research. More senior trainees were preferred by hosts given the short internship duration.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C138 present consistent themes from focus group data about factors affecting internship success. The findings are logical and align with practical considerations about lab productivity and intern readiness. While based on qualitative data, the themes are clearly articulated and supported by the focus group methodology described earlier.

results.result: Important program design features include pre-internship career coaching, an annual poster session at the NC Biotechnology Center, and Scope of Work documents signed by all stakeholders. The Scope of Work details expectations, deliverables, project descriptions, and timelines. Common deliverables include written reports or presentations, with some internships dedicated entirely to specific deliverables like grant writing or competitor analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C149 describe specific, concrete program components that are well-documented. These are operational details of the program rather than research findings, but they are clearly stated and internally consistent. The emphasis on stakeholder agreement (C145-C146) aligns with the program's focus on balancing interests.

results.result: Stakeholder satisfaction was high across all groups. Among hosts: 95% were satisfied, 96% would supervise again, 92% would extend with funding, 98% rated communication as good/very good/excellent, and 73% would offer career positions. Among research advisors: 80% were satisfied, 92% saw neutral/positive impact on research quantity, 96% on research quality, 85% of interns met/exceeded expectations, and 89% would encourage future participation. Interns' independence and communication skills were rated higher than peers (42% and 33% respectively).
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C165 present extensive survey data showing consistently high satisfaction across stakeholder groups. The percentages are specific and supported by Figures 4a-4u. The data is internally consistent and shows alignment between different satisfaction measures. The high ratings across multiple dimensions strengthen confidence in overall program success.

results.result: Alumni interviews revealed that strong alignment between internship and dissertation projects can increase benefits but also introduce tension due to intellectual property concerns. Confidentiality requirements, particularly for industry R&D internships, surprised many research advisors and sometimes frustrated communication. The authors advise choosing internship projects tangential to dissertation research, overlapping on technical level but not scientific questions.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C172 identify a nuanced challenge and provide practical guidance. The tension between alignment benefits and IP concerns is a realistic finding supported by qualitative data. The recommendation (C170-C172) follows logically from the identified problem. This represents thoughtful program refinement based on experience.

results.result: Research advisors indicated they received little communication from internship hosts and would have liked some interaction, though not extensive reports. Survey data showed 79% considered communication with program staff 'sufficient' even though 53% communicated 'never,' 'very rarely,' or 'rarely.' Only 21% indicated insufficient communication, nearly all of whom reported infrequent contact. This suggests effective communication doesn't need to be extensive.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C180 present an interesting finding about communication expectations. The apparent paradox (low frequency but adequate sufficiency) is explained by research advisors not considering extensive communication necessary (C176). The crosstab data in Figure 4u supports this interpretation. The conclusion (C180) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Dynamic federal immigration statutes and university interpretations have made internship participation difficult or impossible for international trainees. The institutional funding model (keeping interns on university payroll) helps with some approvals. Credit-bearing courses can facilitate CPT use, which is more accessible than OPT and can be approved by the university rather than federal government, though this requires additional tuition payment. Alumni interviews suggest international students face particular difficulty transitioning to desired careers even after productive internships.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C190 describe real challenges for international trainees with specific details about visa regulations (CPT vs OPT). The institutional funding advantage (C183) is a logical consequence of the funding model. The alumni interview finding (C190) highlights an important equity concern. These are honest acknowledgments of program limitations for a significant trainee population.

results.result: The ImPACT program was initially funded through savings from UNC's NIH BEST award (2015-2019), then transitioned to UNC School of Medicine institutional funding (2020-present). The funding model was designed to maximize faculty support by not using research advisor grant funds for intern support. The program has experimented with multiple funding streams including grants, industry partnerships, institutional funding, and individual fellowships (F31, F32, NSF GRFP, HHMI Gilliam). Securing university funding as the primary source helps retain control of internship length, critical for sustainability.
results.evaluation: Claims C191-C200 document the funding trajectory and rationale clearly. The successful transition from grant to institutional funding (C191-C192) demonstrates program sustainability. The strategic reasoning about faculty support (C193-C194) is logical. The experimentation with multiple funding models (C195-C198) shows adaptability. The conclusion about university funding benefits (C199) is supported by earlier findings about the importance of internship length control.

results.result: Faculty culture shifted to be more accepting of internships after program implementation, with support increasing substantially for both 1-month and 3-month formats over 5 years. The program successfully transitioned from NIH pilot funding to institutional support, achieving long-term sustainability. The authors attribute increased faculty support to successfully balancing stakeholder interests, particularly keeping internships short and minimizing financial costs to research advisors.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C6, C204, C225, and C226 summarize major program outcomes. The faculty attitude shift is supported by statistical evidence (C115). The funding transition is documented (C191-C192). The interpretation about balancing stakeholder interests (C226) is reasonable given the extensive data on stakeholder satisfaction and the importance of internship length. These represent key achievements of the program.

results.result: The mixed-methods study demonstrated wide-ranging positive results with definitive benefits for all stakeholder groups. Interns found the experience highly valuable (95-97% agreement on key benefits) and were three times more likely to match career interests with first jobs. Career outcomes were positively impacted. The program was designed to minimize negative impacts on research, and 42% of interns reported improved productivity while 33% reported improved quality. No long-term negative effects were detected in publication rates or time to degree, replicating findings from 10 institutions nationally.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C213 provide an accurate summary of major findings. Each statement is supported by specific data presented earlier: high intern satisfaction (C26-C30), career matching (C79-C80), productivity impacts (C32-C33, C109-C111). The replication of productivity findings (C212) strengthens confidence. The conclusion about high cost-benefit ratio (C213) is reasonable given the absence of negative impacts and presence of multiple benefits.

results.result: Internship hosts had positive expectations that were reinforced or exceeded by their experiences. While mentoring was the top initial motivator, hosts found better-than-expected experiences with intern assistance on products and gaining fresh ideas. The expectation of interacting with potential future hires was ranked even more positively than expected by the end of the hosting experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C214-C216 accurately summarize the host experience data presented in C64-C72. The pre-post comparisons with statistical significance (C69-C70) support the conclusion that some benefits exceeded expectations. This is a fair summary of the host stakeholder findings.

results.result: Faculty research advisors, who take on the most risk with least to gain, nonetheless reported tangible benefits in both surveys and focus groups. Indirect benefits include recruiting high-quality, career-motivated students, with professional development offerings consistently rated as a major factor in choosing UNC on recruitment surveys. The program also provides advantages for securing and maintaining institutional training grants like NIH T32 awards.
results.evaluation: Claims C217-C222 acknowledge the challenging position of research advisors while documenting benefits. The recruitment benefit (C220) is supported by unpublished survey data. The T32 advantage (C222) is a logical inference given NIH emphasis on career development. The characterization of research advisors as taking most risk (C217) is reasonable given their dependence on trainee productivity.

results.result: The authors recommend that internship programs encourage trainees to strategize internship timing to maximize gain and minimize productivity impacts, and emphasize that communicating with faculty before and after implementation is critical to gain buy-in, manage expectations, and adjust as needed.
results.evaluation: Claims C223-C224 present reasonable recommendations based on the program's experience. The advice about timing aligns with findings about optimal timing (C135-C137). The emphasis on faculty communication aligns with the faculty attitude change data (C115) and the importance of stakeholder engagement throughout the manuscript.

results.result: The authors address the concern that career exploration might dissuade trainees from academic careers by citing evidence that exploration can lead some trainees to seek academic opportunities once they understand options in detail. They attribute this to non-academic paths holding inflated appeal due to 'grass-is-greener' phenomenon, and argue that experiential exploration provides realistic understanding of workplace realities, making informed career decisions beneficial for both trainees and employers.
results.evaluation: Claims C227-C231 present a counterargument to a common faculty concern. The citation to Layton et al., 2020 (C228) provides evidence for the claim. The 'grass-is-greener' interpretation (C229) is speculative but reasonable. The overall argument is logical and addresses an important stakeholder concern, though the evidence is primarily from citation rather than the current study's data.

results.result: Staff time and personnel effort were cited by some BEST programs as impediments to developing internship programs. At UNC, one PhD-level staff director dedicates about 40% effort as primary program administrator, with another PhD-level director providing support as needed and an active faculty advisor devoting 5-10 hours monthly. The most time-consuming tasks include managing partnerships, communicating with stakeholders, coaching interns, overseeing applications/matching, and coordinating funding.
results.evaluation: Claims C232-C236 provide transparent information about resource requirements. The citation to Lenzi et al., 2020 (C232) contextualizes this as a known challenge. The specific staffing details (C233-C235) are concrete and useful for other institutions. This honest assessment of resource needs is valuable for program replication.

results.result: During the first 5 years, internships were available to both graduate students and postdocs, with postdocs comprising 21% of interns. After 2020, funding mandates no longer allowed postdoc internships. Research advisors of postdoc interns were less supportive for several reasons: 160 hours represents a larger percentage of variable-length postdoc training, some view postdocs as less amenable to career exploration, at-will employment makes abrupt departure more likely, and postdoc salaries are nearly twice graduate stipends. Despite challenges, postdoc interns rated experiences highly and often transitioned to employment with hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C237-C245 honestly document challenges with postdoc internships while acknowledging their value. The reasons for lower research advisor support (C241-C243) are logical. The salary challenge (C244) is a practical concern. The positive postdoc outcomes (C245) despite challenges shows nuanced understanding. The funding change (C238) is a limitation but honestly reported.

results.result: The authors argue that most trainees would benefit from off-campus internships even if planning academic careers, noting internships are ubiquitous in other professional programs (law, business, nursing, computer science, engineering). However, due to resource scarcity and current biomedical training structures, internships remain highly competitive and accessible only to a fraction of trainees at a minority of institutions. Some research advisors view internships as rewards for only the most productive students. The authors expect continued systemic changes to increase access and shift costs away from training programs as internship value becomes more evident.
results.evaluation: Claims C246-C252 provide broader context and future outlook. The comparison to other professional programs (C247) is supported by citation. The acknowledgment of current limitations (C248-C250) is honest and based on focus group data (C250). The expectation of future change (C251) is speculative but reasonable given the evidence presented. The hope for broader adoption (C252) is appropriate for a discussion section.

results.result: The authors compare their model to other successful programs, including UCSF (which places interns after dissertation defense/graduation), and other models involving shorter, unpaid, or company-paid internships. They note their model's benefit of occurring mid-training allows follow-up skill-building before job market entry, but acknowledge the delay between internship and start date could be a downside for companies viewing internships as hiring mechanisms. They recommend future work evaluating whether stakeholder benefits and faculty buy-in differ across models.
results.evaluation: Claims C253-C258 provide appropriate context by comparing to other models with citations (C253, C255). The analysis of tradeoffs (C254, C257-C258) shows thoughtful consideration of different approaches. The recommendation for comparative research (C256) is appropriate. This demonstrates scholarly awareness of alternative approaches.

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations to generalizability including differing institutional climates, local economic environments, and employer availability. They note different funding structures may better fit different universities and call for future studies evaluating different funding models. They address geographic challenges for institutions not near biotech/pharma hubs, suggesting alternatives including virtual internships, partnerships with distant institutions, traveling to biotech hubs (piloted by University of Chicago and Vanderbilt), or emphasizing transferrable skills for local economic opportunities.
results.evaluation: Claims C259-C267 provide honest acknowledgment of limitations and practical suggestions for adaptation. The geographic challenge is real and the suggested alternatives are reasonable. The citations to other programs (C265, C267) show these alternatives have been tested. The call for future research (C261) is appropriate. This demonstrates thoughtful consideration of generalizability.

results.result: The authors acknowledge self-selection bias as a potential limitation, noting interns may differ from non-participants in career goal clarity, motivation, or research advisor support. They suggest a randomized controlled trial with various experiential learning options could identify most beneficial programmatic elements, with trainees ethically randomized to different career development opportunities. However, they note that once a program shows definitive benefits, it becomes unethical to assign people to control conditions depriving them of that opportunity. They recommend future research on creating universally available internship opportunities fully integrated into graduate training.
results.evaluation: Claims C268-C273 demonstrate appropriate scientific caution about causal inference. The acknowledgment of self-selection bias (C268-C269) is important and honest. The RCT suggestion (C270-C271) is methodologically sound. The ethical consideration (C272) shows awareness of research ethics. The recommendation for universal access (C273) is aspirational but appropriate. This represents thoughtful consideration of study limitations and future directions.

results.result: The authors note that reflection is a key component of experiential learning and suggest that while trainees reflected during program evaluation, more structured guided reflection might provide additional benefits. They recommend future studies systematically examine whether additional post-internship or ongoing reflections during internships provide richer perspectives. They also suggest future studies should examine faculty support at other institutions since training culture and perspectives vary across institutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C274-C277 identify areas for program enhancement and research. The emphasis on reflection is supported by citation (C274). The suggestions for more structured reflection (C275-C276) are reasonable program improvements. The call for multi-institutional research (C277) acknowledges generalizability concerns. These are appropriate recommendations for future work.

results.result: The authors note that global events including COVID-19 increased the need for creative experiential career development opportunities. During later cohorts, the program adapted to changing workforce needs, job market trends, and limitations on in-person opportunities. As the program emerged from pandemic impacts, it entered a phase of increased hiring and high opportunity (the 'Great Resignation'). Future directions include expanding territories, developing partnerships, job location flexibility (remote/hybrid/in-person), adjusting to company needs while meeting trainee interests, and multiple funding models for sustainability.
results.evaluation: Claims C278-C282 describe program adaptation to external circumstances. The COVID-19 impact is supported by citation (C278). The description of program adaptation (C279) demonstrates flexibility. The reference to the Great Resignation (C280) is supported by citation. The future directions (C281-C282) are reasonable extensions of the program. This shows program resilience and forward thinking.

results.result: The authors conclude that internship programs for PhD and postdoctoral life scientists provide myriad benefits to interns, research advisors' lab climate and productivity, and host organizations. They argue that customized programs maximizing institutional resources, location, and partner access can achieve sustainability. They emphasize that implementation aligning and balancing all stakeholder interests while securing research advisor support is critical to program success.
results.evaluation: Claims C283-C285 provide appropriate summary conclusions supported by the extensive data presented throughout the manuscript. The emphasis on stakeholder balance (C285) is a key theme supported by the satisfaction data and faculty attitude changes. The conclusion about sustainability (C284) is supported by the successful funding transition. These are well-supported summary statements.

results.result: The authors describe the development and implementation of the ImPACT internship program at UNC, which over 5 years placed 123 interns at over 70 partner sites representing at least 20 career paths. The program structure includes 160-hour internships, requires research advisor support and completion of qualifying exams, and has successfully transitioned from NIH BEST grant funding to institutional support.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm the program description, noting 'the internship program is well described' and 'outcomes are clearly defined.' The editor states the study 'evaluates the outcomes of a single-institution pilot program' with good sample size (123 internships) and high response rates, indicating acceptance of the program's scope and structure.

results.result: Survey data from interns showed overwhelmingly positive outcomes: 90% were highly satisfied, 97% agreed the internship provided unique networking opportunities, 95% felt it increased job market competitiveness, and understanding of career benefits/challenges doubled from pre- to post-internship (48% to 97%, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. The editor notes the data 'convincingly show the benefit of internships to students and postdocs,' and the anonymous reviewer acknowledges 'the overall finding support the hypothesis' of benefits to interns. The high response rates (66% for interns) are noted as minimizing potential bias.

results.result: Logistic regression analysis demonstrated that internship participation significantly predicted career interest-job placement match (OR=2.99, p<0.001), meaning interns were nearly three times more likely to match their career interests than non-interns. The model controlled for number of career interests and trainee type, with 39% of interns achieving exact matches versus 29% of non-interns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accept these career outcomes findings. The editor states the data 'convincingly show the benefit' and the anonymous reviewer notes 'students who did internships were significantly less likely to pursue postdoctoral fellowships' and 'were more likely to have science-related careers,' though acknowledging 'the study design cannot determine whether this is a causal relationship.'

results.result: Career outcomes analysis showed that 36% of interns pursued postdoctoral training compared to 57% of non-interns. Interns were more likely to enter for-profit sectors (75% vs 42%) and science-related careers (37% vs 24%) compared to non-interns, with fewer entering academic positions (19% vs 46%).
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly acknowledges these findings, stating 'students who did internships were significantly less likely to pursue postdoctoral fellowships before entering the biomedical workforce and were more likely to have science-related careers versus research careers than control students who did not do internships,' though noting the observational design limits causal inference.

results.result: Analysis of trainee productivity showed no negative impact from internship participation: interns had slightly more first-author publications and slightly fewer total publications (neither statistically significant), average time to degree was 67.1 months for interns vs 69.3 months for controls (p=0.09), and 42% of interns reported improved research productivity while 92% of research advisors reported neutral or positive impact on research quantity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly affirm these findings. The editor states the data show benefits 'without adverse impacts on scientific productivity,' and the anonymous reviewer notes 'the data refute one of the principle concerns of research advisors: that by taking students out of the lab, internships reduce individual and overall lab productivity.' The reviewer calls this finding useful 'to dispel some of the concerns of research advisers.'

results.result: Faculty attitudes toward internships improved significantly over 5 years of program implementation. Support for 1-month internships increased from 86% to 92% (t(212)=2.00, p<0.01) and for 3-month internships from 68% to 75% (t(229)=2.54, p=0.01), with decreases in 'highly unlikely' and 'unlikely' responses and increases in 'highly likely' responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. The editor notes the study demonstrates benefits 'to research advisors' and the anonymous reviewer states the paper 'will be very useful for other institutions to dispel some of the concerns of research advisers about internships for PhD students,' implicitly accepting the faculty attitude shift data.

results.result: Research advisors reported multiple benefits from the internship program: 96% indicated positive impact on interns' competitiveness, 80% noted improved communication with their trainee, and qualitative data revealed benefits including enhanced lab motivation, new technical skills brought back to the lab, improved lab culture, and opportunities for industry collaborations. Nearly 80% were satisfied with the program and 89% would encourage future participation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the overall positive outcomes. The editor states the data show benefits 'to research advisors' and the anonymous reviewer notes 'the overall finding support the hypothesis' including benefits to research advisors. The reviewer acknowledges 'positive impact for the lab, improved communication between the intern and their research advisor' as additional benefits.

results.result: Internship hosts reported high satisfaction (95%) and multiple benefits that often exceeded expectations: 89% experienced fulfillment from mentoring, 83% attracted quality applicants, and interaction with potential future hires increased significantly from pre- to post-internship (p<0.001). Nearly three-quarters (73%) were highly likely to offer interns career positions, and 96% would supervise another intern.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. The editor states the data 'convincingly show the benefit of internships to...potential employers,' and the anonymous reviewer notes 'positive outcomes for hosts' and suggests 'industry will be motivated to support internships by the positive outcomes for hosts reported in this paper.'

results.result: Research advisors strongly preferred 1-month full-time internships over longer formats, viewing them as least disruptive to lab progress. Support consistently dropped as internship length increased from 1 to 3 months. Advisors considered trainee abilities, timing (preferably near graduation during writing phase), and organizational skills when determining internship appropriateness.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept these findings through their acknowledgment of the program's design features. The anonymous reviewer notes the study provides 'lessons learned for other institutions seeking to create their own internship programs' and that the paper will help 'dispel some of the concerns of research advisers,' suggesting acceptance of the timing and structure findings.

results.result: Important program design features identified by stakeholders included pre-internship career coaching to frame internships as skill-building experiences, an annual poster session at the NC Biotechnology Center for networking and program visibility, and Scope of Work documents signed by all parties detailing project expectations and deliverables.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these design elements as part of the well-described program. The anonymous reviewer notes 'the internship program is well described' and lists as a strength that 'outcomes are clearly defined,' implicitly accepting the program structure and design features described.

results.result: The program's funding model, where interns remain on institutional payroll rather than research advisor grants, was designed to maximize faculty support. Funding transitioned from NIH BEST grant support (2015-2019) to institutional support from the UNC School of Medicine (2020-present). The authors explored multiple funding streams including fellowships (F31, F32, NSF, HHMI) and found institutional funding helps retain control of internship length.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the funding model description without challenge. The anonymous reviewer explicitly notes that 'wider adoption of internships as part of PhD training will depend not only on faculty buy-in but also on availability of resources and changes to the graduate school funding model,' and suggests 'NIH could allow a certain amount of F, T, or even RPG funds to be used to support internships,' indicating engagement with and acceptance of the funding discussion.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that trainees who elect to do internships are a self-selected population with career biases—they are less likely to want academic tenure-track positions, more likely to have for-profit aspirations, and must have research advisor support. This self-selection bias is a potential limitation of the observational study design.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly acknowledges this limitation, stating 'the authors acknowledge that limitation that the study subjects were self-selected and also had research advisors who agreed to allow them to participate. Thus the generally favorable outcomes may not be applicable to students such as those who are struggling in the lab and/or lack career focus or supportive research advisors.'

results.result: Dynamic federal immigration statutes and university interpretations created challenges for international trainees participating in internships. The institutional payroll model helped with some approvals, and credit-bearing courses enabled use of Curricular Practical Training (CPT), though this required additional tuition. Alumni interviews suggested international students faced particular difficulties transitioning to desired careers even after productive internships.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly comment on these challenges, but their acceptance of the overall study methodology and acknowledgment of limitations suggests implicit acceptance of these described operational challenges as part of the program's context.

results.result: During the first 5 years, postdocs comprised 21% of interns, but after 2020 the funding mandate no longer allowed postdoctoral internships. Research advisors of postdoc interns were less supportive due to concerns about the internship representing a greater percentage of training time, postdocs being more likely to leave abruptly if offered positions, and higher salary costs. However, postdoc interns rated experiences highly and often transitioned to employment with hosts.
results.evaluation: The anonymous reviewer explicitly notes the findings may not apply 'to postdoctoral fellows' and states the paper will be useful 'to dispel some of the concerns of research advisers about internships for PhD students (although not necessarily for postdoctoral fellows),' indicating acceptance of the differential outcomes and challenges for postdocs described by the authors.

results.result: Program administration requires one PhD-level staff director dedicating approximately 40% full-time effort to managing partnerships, communications, coaching, applications, and funding coordination, with additional support from another PhD-level director and an active faculty advisor devoting 5-10 hours per month.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly comment on staffing details, but the anonymous reviewer's acknowledgment that 'wider adoption of internships as part of PhD training will depend not only on faculty buy-in but also on availability of resources' suggests implicit acceptance of the resource requirements described, including staffing needs.

results.result: The authors acknowledge limitations to generalizability including differing institutional climates, local economic environments, and employer availability. They suggest future studies should evaluate different funding models and note that geographic challenges could be overcome through virtual internships, travel to biotech hubs, or partnerships emphasizing transferable skills in local economic opportunities.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these acknowledged limitations. The anonymous reviewer's statement that the paper provides 'lessons learned for other institutions seeking to create their own internship programs' and discussion of broader implementation challenges suggests acceptance of the generalizability limitations and alternative approaches described.

results.result: The authors suggest future research directions including randomized controlled trials comparing different experiential learning options, ways to integrate internships for all students, more structured post-internship reflection components, and studies of faculty support at other institutions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these suggestions for future research. The editor's statement that the work 'should stimulate further research into how such programs can best be broadly implemented' aligns with and implicitly supports the authors' suggestions for future studies.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate program description and scope (C1-C3, C19-C24). OpenEval finds detailed, consistent documentation of program design. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'the internship program is well described' and note good sample size and response rates. Strong agreement on program description quality.

Both assess intern survey outcomes (C26-C38). OpenEval finds data supported with appropriate statistics and adequate response rates. Peer reviewers accept findings without challenge, with editor noting data 'convincingly show the benefit of internships to students and postdocs.' Strong agreement on intern benefits.

Both address qualitative focus group findings (C39-C63). OpenEval emphasizes mixed-methods strength and longitudinal design. Peer reviewers accept findings as part of overall positive outcomes, noting benefits to research advisors and improved communication. Agreement on qualitative data value.

Both evaluate host/employer outcomes (C64-C72). OpenEval finds nuanced, credible pre-post data with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers accept findings, with editor noting data show benefits 'to potential employers' and reviewer noting 'positive outcomes for hosts.' Strong agreement.

Both assess career matching logistic regression (C73-C90). OpenEval finds well-designed analysis with appropriate controls and substantial effect size. Peer reviewers acknowledge findings but note 'the study design cannot determine whether this is a causal relationship.' Agreement on findings with shared caution about causality.

Both evaluate career outcome differences (C91-C106). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to self-selection bias acknowledged by authors. Peer reviewers accept descriptive findings (lower postdoc rates, more science-related careers) while also noting observational design limits causal inference. Strong agreement on limitation.

Both assess productivity/publication outcomes (C107-C111). OpenEval finds appropriate statistical comparisons showing no evidence of harm. Peer reviewers strongly affirm, with editor noting benefits 'without adverse impacts on scientific productivity' and reviewer stating data 'refute one of the principle concerns of research advisors.' Strong agreement.

Both evaluate faculty attitude changes (C112-C117). OpenEval finds clear pre-post comparison with appropriate statistics. Peer reviewers accept finding, with reviewer noting paper 'will be very useful...to dispel some of the concerns of research advisers.' Strong agreement on faculty shift.

Both address internship timing and structure preferences (C121, C125-C138). OpenEval finds consistency across data sources on optimal duration. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through acknowledgment of 'lessons learned for other institutions' and program design features. Agreement on structural findings.

Both evaluate factors affecting internship success (C131-C138). OpenEval finds logical, well-articulated qualitative themes. Peer reviewers implicitly accept as part of 'lessons learned' that will help other institutions. Agreement on practical guidance.

Both assess program operational components (C139-C149). OpenEval finds concrete, well-documented program features. Peer reviewers accept as part of well-described program with 'clearly defined' outcomes. Strong agreement on program structure.

Both evaluate satisfaction data across stakeholders (C150-C165). OpenEval finds extensive, consistent high satisfaction with specific percentages. Peer reviewers accept as part of convincing benefit demonstration. Agreement on satisfaction outcomes, though peer review emphasizes host satisfaction specifically.
